families.title: What can a flow map actually tell you?
families.core_gate: Area, speed and volume units; multiplication, division and weighted means. Algebra describes every branch split. A storage ledger is the core conservation argument.
families.index_gate: Area × mean speed, weighted means and conservation; algebra for every branch split
families.extension_gate: Vector calculus and the divergence theorem for the local continuity equation. Density and mass-rate arithmetic for the compressible continuation.
families.reading: Short labeled flow diagrams; a facilitator may read rules aloud. Distinguish a point speed, section mean normal speed, volume rate and mass rate.
families.materials: Pencil, ruler, optional equal-volume blocks; supplied tube, split-section and branch diagrams. All arrows label mean normal speed unless a patch is explicitly uniform. No running-water demonstration is needed.
families.timing: 0–8 move equal-volume packets through two gates; 8–20 design and reject section labels; 20–35 compare velocity profiles; 35–50 classify branch choices; later 20 minutes for changed storage/density models. Hand out one page at a time.
families.launch: A wide gate passes 12 volume units each second. Can a narrow gate carry that same flow? Make a plausible-looking label that the stored-water count exposes.
families.satisfying_stop: A conservation certificate rejects a map, while explicit distinct profiles and branch splits show what the same certificate leaves undetermined.
families.prior_use: Week 10 and trial GA-25 concern graph traversal or trees. This is material flux and underdetermination, not another route puzzle. AP-30 later uses an analogous conservation law plus constitutive information; cross-link that distinction.
families.assessment: Promising with fractions and units. The finite section/branch argument is a real conservation special case; the vector-calculus extension remains advanced. Physical model assumptions need explicit adult reading.
families.mathematical_connection: Integral conservation, weighted means and an affine family of admissible fluxes. Passing continuity is a necessary test, not a solution of momentum, pressure or viscosity equations.

pages.title: Catch an impossible label
pages.gate: Core: area, speed and volume per time
pages.intro: A rigid full tube carries constant-density liquid steadily, with no leaks. At a cross-section, Q = area × mean forward normal speed. Q is volume per second. If speeds vary, use the area-weighted mean.

prompts.text: The wide section has area 6 and mean speed 2. The narrow section has area 3. Invent one possible and one impossible narrow mean-speed label. For the impossible label, explain where the volume count fails after one second.
prompts.solution: Incoming Q=12. The only conserving narrow mean is 4. Any nonnegative speed w≠4 fails: the intervening inventory changes at rate 12−3w. For example w=3 gives a gain of 3 volume units per second; w=5 requires a loss of 3. Both contradict a steady rigid full tube with constant-density liquid and no leaks. Equal Q passes only this necessary conservation test, not all fluid equations.
hints: Count the volume crossing each gate in one second.
Keep a ledger for the region between the gates.

prompts.text: Split the narrow section into patches of areas 1 and 2, each with a uniform forward speed. Design two different nonnegative speed pairs that carry the required flow. Then test patch speeds 2 and 5. Is the ordinary average of those two readings the section mean?
prompts.solution: Patch speeds u,v satisfy u+2v=12. Examples (0,6), (8,2), and (4,4) all work; the complete nonnegative family has 0≤v≤6 and u=12−2v. For (2,5), Q=1×2+2×5=12, so the section mean is 12/3=4, while the unweighted average is 7/2. A local fast reading does not determine Q. These piecewise-uniform profiles are section data for the conservation audit, not asserted viscous solutions.
hints: The larger patch contributes twice as much area.
Try keeping the weighted sum fixed while changing the two speeds.

pages.title: A branch does not choose its own flow
pages.gate: Core continuation: classify a nonnegative family
pages.intro: The same incoming volume rate 12 now splits into two steady outlets with areas 2 and 1. Their mean forward speeds are u and v. There are no other outlets or storage changes.

prompts.text: Design two conserving splits: in one, the smaller outlet is faster; in the other, it is slower. Describe EVERY nonnegative pair (u,v) that passes the conservation test. What are the largest possible u and v?
prompts.solution: Conservation is 2u+v=12, with u,v≥0. For example (u,v)=(2,8) has the smaller outlet faster; (5,2) has it slower. Every solution is v=12−2u with 0≤u≤6. Thus max u=6 at v=0 and max v=12 at u=0. Zero flow is permitted by the stated nonnegative convention. Narrower-implies-faster required equal Q in a single stream tube; separate branches need not have equal Q.
hints: Add the two outgoing volume rates.
Describe the allowed portion of a line, including its endpoints.

prompts.text: A designer says, “The areas alone determine both speeds.” Refute that claim with a certificate. Then a sensor reports u=4. What does this additional observation determine? Does it determine the pressure?
prompts.solution: The two distinct pairs in prompt 3 are an explicit nonuniqueness certificate for the same incoming rate and areas. With u=4, conservation gives v=4, and outgoing rates are 8 and 4. It still does not determine pressure: no force, energy, viscosity or boundary-pressure law has been supplied. Distinct pressure/velocity-profile details are not excluded by this ledger.
hints: Which unknowns occur in the conservation equation?
A new measured speed is different from a new physical law.

pages.title: Which assumption changed?
pages.gate: Continuation: storage and mass density
pages.intro: Keep an observed inlet volume rate 12 and outlet volume rate 9. Change the model explicitly in each task. Rates and dimensions use consistent units.

prompts.text: Replace the rigid full tube by a tank with horizontal area 4, initial volume 8 and capacity 20. The two rates remain constant; there is no leak. Predict the water-level rise per second and the first overflow time. Could the same two flow readings alone prove that a pipe has a leak?
prompts.solution: Before overflow, volume is V(t)=8+(12−9)t=8+3t. Height is V/4, so its rate is 3/4 length unit per second; initial height is 2 and rim height is 5. Capacity is reached at t=4 seconds; overflow begins thereafter. The readings alone do not identify a leak: changing stored volume is another explanation. Under the original steady, full, constant-density assumptions, a third outlet of rate 3 would balance the ledger. The two explanations rely on different stated models.
hints: A volume increase divided by horizontal area is a height increase.
Compare the inventory change with the unaccounted boundary flow.

prompts.text: Now use a steady compressible gas in a rigid tube, with uniform density at each section. Inlet density is 1; its area is 6 and mean speed is 2. Outlet area is 3 and mean speed is 3. Choose an outlet density that conserves MASS. Explain why conserving volume would give the wrong test here.
prompts.solution: Mass rate is density×area×mean normal speed when section density is uniform. Inlet mass rate is 12, outlet is 9ρ, so ρ=4/3 is required. Volume rates 12 and 9 differ without steady mass accumulation because the gas is denser downstream. This is a continuity-compatible data set, not a proof of a full gas-dynamical solution. Constant-density incompressibility was deliberately removed.
hints: Track mass carried by each unit of volume.
Do not assume the inlet and outlet densities agree.

extensions.gate: Partial derivatives, integration and the divergence theorem.
extensions.prompt: Derive the control-volume mass law from ∂ρ/∂t + div(ρu)=0. For constant density, test u=(ax,by) on the rectangle 0≤x≤2, 0≤y≤1 per unit depth. Which a,b pass local incompressibility?
extensions.solution: For a fixed region V, differentiation under the integral and the divergence theorem give d/dt ∫Vρ dV=−∫∂Vρu·n dA. With spatially and temporally constant positive ρ, div u=0. Here div u=a+b; hence b=−a. Right-edge outward volume flux is (2a)×1=2a, top-edge flux b×2=2b, and the x=0/y=0 edge fluxes are zero, so total outward flux is 2(a+b). This rectangle is a control region with permeable boundaries, not an impermeable-wall tube. The family (x,−y) passes; (x,y) fails. This supplies no momentum solution.

figures.student_workspace: Two unlabeled patch-profile attempts; open speed-pair plane and explanation area. Do not draw the solution segment or its endpoints in advance. Diagram labels distinguish Q and mean speed.

families.title: Choose the fastest crossing
families.core_gate: Pythagoras and distance/speed for the launch; derivatives and a global monotonicity or convexity argument are required for the satisfying optimum.
families.index_gate: Pythagoras and calculus: certify a continuous optimum and design its speed ratio
families.extension_gate: Implicit or monotonic comparative reasoning for changing a medium speed; no wave-boundary or diffraction theorem is claimed.
families.reading: Coordinate pairs, square roots, derivatives and angles measured from the normal. Calculators may support experiments but not replace the continuum proof.
families.materials: Supplied coordinate diagrams, ruler and a movable crossing marker; optional calculator. The upper and lower regions have constant positive speeds. No actual water is needed.
families.timing: 0–12 choose crossings and compare time with distance; 12–30 derive and certify the optimum; 30–45 handle a restricted crossing gate; 45–60 design a new speed. The calculus proof is core, not an optional decoration.
families.launch: Travel from A=(0,4) to B=(7,−3). Above the shoreline speed is 3; below it speed is 4. Choose where to cross. A shorter-looking route may take longer.
families.satisfying_stop: A unique global minimizing crossing, a correct boundary optimum when access is restricted, and an inverse construction making a chosen crossing optimal.
families.prior_use: Week 9 reflections and GA-21 mirror optimization use equal-speed reflected distance. This is unequal-speed refraction, with an actual derivative law and a different inverse-design problem.
families.assessment: Advanced/specialist calculus investigation. The trial stage is accessible with roots and ratios, but alone is not marketed as a proof of the real optimization.
families.mathematical_connection: Strict convexity of a sum of weighted distances, Snell’s sine law from a stationary time, and constrained versus unconstrained optima.

pages.title: Race time, not distance
pages.gate: Calculus core; Pythagoras starts the experiment
pages.intro: A=(0,4), B=(7,−3). A permitted route is a straight segment from A to C=(x,0), then a straight segment to B. Any real x is allowed. Speeds are constant: 3 above y=0 and 4 below. Crossing takes no extra time.

prompts.text: Choose two crossing points and compare both total distance and total time. Find where the direct straight line from A to B crosses. Must that shortest route also be fastest?
prompts.solution: For any x, lengths are L1=√(x²+16), L2=√((7−x)²+9), distance L1+L2 and time T=L1/3+L2/4. Any correctly calculated chosen trials are acceptable. The direct line crosses at x=4 because its vertical drop to y=0 is 4/7 of the total drop 7. At x=4, lengths are 4√2 and 3√2, so distance 7√2 and time 25√2/12. At x=3, lengths 5,5, distance 10 and time 35/12. Since 35<25√2 (1225<1250), x=3 is faster despite 10>7√2. This comparison disproves fastest=shortest here, before the full optimum is proved.
hints: Use distance divided by the speed on that side.
Compare a convenient pair of right triangles.

prompts.text: Build T(x) from the picture. Find a candidate crossing that cannot be improved by a tiny move either way. Give an exact time, not just a graph estimate.
prompts.solution: T(x)=√(x²+16)/3+√((7−x)²+9)/4. Its derivative is x/[3√(x²+16)]−(7−x)/[4√((7−x)²+9)]. At x=3 the two terms are 3/15 and 4/20, both 1/5, so T′(3)=0 and T(3)=35/12. A stationary calculation alone is not yet a global certificate; prompt 3 supplies that.
hints: Differentiate both distance terms, keeping the minus sign in 7−x.
Look for two 3–4–5 triangles.

pages.title: Certify the best route
pages.gate: Calculus: a global guarantee and endpoint constraints
pages.intro: A stationary value is a candidate. Your certificate must cover every allowed crossing, including points outside the segment from x=0 to x=7.

prompts.text: Prove that your best crossing is the ONLY global minimizer over all real x. Then express its derivative balance using the two angles from the vertical normal.
prompts.solution: T″(x)=16/[3(x²+16)^(3/2)]+9/[4((7−x)²+9)^(3/2)]>0 for every real x. Hence T′ is strictly increasing, negative for x<3 and positive for x>3, since T′(3)=0. By the mean value theorem T decreases then increases, proving the unique global minimum. At the optimum 0<x<7, sin θ1=x/L1 and sin θ2=(7−x)/L2, with both acute angles measured from the normal. The equation is sin θ1/3=sin θ2/4; here θ1 has sine 3/5 and θ2 has sine 4/5. No total-internal-reflection claim follows from this endpoint problem.
hints: Can you show the derivative changes in only one direction?
Mark the horizontal component of each unit direction.

prompts.text: A fence permits crossing only on the closed interval 4≤x≤6. Choose the fastest allowed crossing and prove it. Does the derivative have to vanish at this new winner?
prompts.solution: T′>0 throughout [4,6], so the unique constrained minimum is x=4, with T=25√2/12. Its derivative does not vanish: T′(4)=1/(3√2)−1/(4√2)=1/(12√2)>0. A boundary minimum need not have zero derivative because the improving leftward direction is forbidden. The certificate uses the allowed interval, not a new physical refraction law.
hints: Where does the unconstrained optimum lie relative to the gate?
Which direction could lower time, and is it permitted?

pages.title: Design the medium to fit your crossing
pages.gate: Calculus and algebra: inverse design
pages.intro: Remove the fence. Keep A, B and the upper speed 3. You may choose any finite positive lower speed w.

prompts.text: Choose a target crossing s strictly between 0 and 7. Find a lower speed w that makes it the unique fastest crossing. Verify your own choice; also recover the original example.
prompts.solution: Stationarity requires s/[3√(s²+16)]=(7−s)/[w√((7−s)²+9)]. Thus w=3(7−s)√(s²+16)/[s√((7−s)²+9)], positive and finite for 0<s<7. The same positive-second-derivative proof works for every w>0, so this is the unique global minimizer. At s=3 it gives w=4; at s=4 it gives w=3. Arbitrary learner targets are verified by substitution into this formula and the positivity argument.
hints: Solve the derivative balance for the speed you control.
A stationary design still needs the same global certificate.

prompts.text: Could a finite positive w make x=0 or x=7 the unconstrained winner? If w increases from 4, predict which way the winner moves and justify the direction.
prompts.solution: T′(0)=−7/[w√58]<0 and T′(7)=7/[3√65]>0, so neither endpoint can be optimal. For every positive finite w, strict increase of T′ and these endpoint signs give one root in (0,7). Increasing w makes the negative second term smaller in magnitude, so T′ at the old root becomes positive. The new unique root must lie to its left. Faster travel below the boundary shifts the crossing toward A, spending less distance in the slower upper medium. Limits w→∞ and w→0+ approach x=0 and x=7 respectively, without attaining either at finite positive w.
hints: Check the derivative at the endpoints directly.
Evaluate the new derivative at the old optimal point.

extensions.gate: Calculus, positive parameters and strict convexity.
extensions.prompt: Replace the heights by a,b>0, horizontal separation by d>0 and speeds by v1,v2>0. Prove the optimizer lies strictly between 0 and d and state the constrained answer for any closed gate [L,U], L≤U.
extensions.solution: T=√(x²+a²)/v1+√((d−x)²+b²)/v2 has T″=a²/[v1(x²+a²)^(3/2)]+b²/[v2((d−x)²+b²)^(3/2)]>0. T′(0)<0 and T′(d)>0, so there is a unique root x*∈(0,d), with T decreasing before it and increasing after it. The constrained minimum is x* when it lies in [L,U], L when x*<L, and U when x*>U, including the single-point gate. This proves a global minimum for the stipulated route class; it does not establish all of wave optics.

families.title: A dimmer signal, a hidden phase
families.core_gate: Signed waveform addition, sine/cosine and squares. The full investigation needs trigonometric addition and a two-coordinate representation; period averages are supplied explicitly.
families.index_gate: Coherent wave addition and trigonometry; use a reference to recover a hidden phase
families.extension_gate: Integration proves the supplied period averages; averaging over an explicitly uniform drifting phase gives an incoherent comparison.
families.reading: Phase is an angle in radians, not a time delay in arbitrary units. Follow a shared time coordinate and distinguish the total signed field from its squared average.
families.materials: Supplied sine/cosine templates, tracing paper or pencil, unit-circle diagram and blank resultant plots. A ruler suffices; no sound or laser apparatus is needed.
families.timing: 0–12 add in-phase and opposite-phase strips; 12–25 compare detector readings; 25–45 derive the phase formula and its attainable range; later 25 minutes for the inverse phase experiment.
families.launch: Two nonzero signals arrive at one detector. You can shift the second one. Can its arrival make the detector less bright? Can brightness alone reveal the shift?
families.satisfying_stop: A complete brightness range and a deliberately chosen extra reference signal that removes a genuine two-phase ambiguity.
families.prior_use: GA-14 later examines temporal aliasing and GA-15 orthogonal signal coordinates. This family asks what coherent intensity loses and how a phase-controlled reference restores it, not just how to add a waveform.
families.assessment: Promising with explicit trigonometry. Pointwise cancellation is a useful earlier stop, but the phase-identification proof is the full core. Scalar same-frequency coherence must remain visible.
families.mathematical_connection: A coherent amplitude pair is a plane vector; squared detector output loses direction. Two controlled intensity observations recover both phase coordinates, with a consistency circle.

sources.title: David Tong, Electromagnetism
sources.adaptation: Use linear same-frequency wave superposition and the quadratic, period-averaged field signal. The normalization and reference-wave inverse problem are defined and proved here.
sources.checked: Reopened 2026-09-25: inspected sine-wave solutions, phase/polarization representation, superposition and average sin²=1/2 in the Poynting calculation. The worksheet fixes one scalar component at one location; no whole-field energy inference is made.

pages.title: Add a signal and reduce the reading
pages.gate: Core launch: signed heights and squared amplitude
pages.intro: At one detector, two coherent scalar waves have the same fixed frequency and polarization. Their signed readings add. A(t)=2 sin t. You may add B(t)=sin(t+φ). Start with φ=0 or π. For E(t)=C sin t, define normalized brightness I=C².

prompts.text: Choose the alignment that you think will dim the detector. Draw the summed waveform over one whole period. Compare A alone with BOTH permitted alignments. Explain using the signed heights, before using brightness.
prompts.solution: For φ=0, B=sin t and E=3 sin t, so I=9. For φ=π, B=−sin t and E=sin t, so I=1. A alone has I=4. The opposite-phase signal therefore reduces the local reading although its own amplitude is nonzero. Each equality holds at every time, not only at plotted sample points. Waveform templates share the same scale and time axis; sum corresponding signed heights.
hints: A negative height subtracts from a positive height.
Check a peak, a trough and an ordinary intermediate time.

prompts.text: You may now change B’s amplitude as well as its phase. Design a nonzero B that makes the total signal zero for the whole period. Does a zero reading here tell you that energy vanished everywhere?
prompts.solution: Choose B(t)=−2 sin t, equivalently amplitude 2 and phase π, so E(t)=0 pointwise. Among B=b sin(t+φ) with b>0, exact cancellation requires b cos φ=−2 and b sin φ=0, hence b=2 and φ=π modulo 2π. No conclusion about energy everywhere follows from this one-detector scalar model. The spatial field, sources and energy transport have not been specified; local cancellation is the stated result.
hints: Match both size and opposite sign, not just a single zero crossing.
Which locations does the supplied model describe?

pages.title: Which brightness values are possible?
pages.gate: Core: sine addition and a complete range
pages.intro: Return to amplitude 1 for B, and allow any real phase φ. Define I=2 times the average of E(t)² over a full period. You may use these exact averages: average(sin² t)=average(cos² t)=1/2; average(sin t cos t)=0.

prompts.text: Write E(t)=P sin t+Q cos t. Use the supplied averages to derive I as a function of φ. Find the least and greatest possible brightness, and show that every value between them can occur.
prompts.solution: Sine addition gives P=2+cos φ and Q=sin φ. Expanding the square and applying the stated averages gives I=P²+Q²=(2+cos φ)²+sin² φ=5+4 cos φ. Since cos φ takes every value in [−1,1], the exact range is [1,9]. The minimum 1 occurs at φ=π modulo 2π and maximum 9 at φ=0 modulo 2π. For any target i∈[1,9], choose a phase with cos φ=(i−5)/4; such a phase exists. In particular, amplitude-1 B can never cancel amplitude-2 A completely.
hints: Keep the cross term until you average it.
On the unit circle, what range can the horizontal coordinate take?

prompts.text: Choose a target brightness strictly between 1 and 9 and find two different phases in [0,2π) that produce it. Describe every phase that makes the detector dimmer than A alone. What information did squaring and averaging lose?
prompts.solution: For a chosen target i∈(1,9), set c=(i−5)/4∈(−1,1). The two phases are arccos c and 2π−arccos c, distinct in [0,2π); they have opposite sine but equal cosine. A convenient choice i=5 gives π/2 and 3π/2. Dimming means 5+4 cos φ<4, or cos φ<−1/4: on [0,2π) the open interval (arccos(−1/4),2π−arccos(−1/4)). For all real phases, take this interval and all its translates by 2πk, k∈Z. Equality at its endpoints gives the original brightness 4. The first observation recovers cosine but loses the sign of sine, and hence generally does not identify phase.
hints: Compare phases reflected across the horizontal axis.
Translate “dimmer than 4” into an inequality for cosine.

pages.title: Design a second observation
pages.gate: Core continuation: recover what the first measurement lost
pages.intro: The unknown phase stays fixed while you repeat the experiment on identically prepared signals. You may add a known coherent reference R(t). All intensities use the same full-period normalization and unchanged amplitude scale.

prompts.text: A first reading gives I=5. Choose ONE reference, R(t)=sin t or R(t)=cos t, that distinguishes the compatible phases modulo 2π. Predict the second reading in each case. Explain why the other reference fails.
prompts.solution: I=5 gives cos φ=0, so φ is π/2 or 3π/2 modulo 2π and E=2 sin t±cos t. Adding R=cos t yields E+R=2 sin t+2 cos t in the plus case (brightness 8), and 2 sin t in the minus case (brightness 4). Adding R=sin t yields 3 sin t±cos t, brightness 10 in both cases, so it fails. This is a controlled repeat with stable relative phase, not a claim that unrelated experimental runs share an unknown phase.
hints: Which coordinate changed sign between the two hidden candidates?
A useful reference must interact with that coordinate.

prompts.text: Let J be the second reading after adding R(t)=cos t. Derive a rule that recovers both cos φ and sin φ from I,J. Decode I=37/5, J=10. Could I=5, J=6 come from this exact model? Give a certificate.
prompts.solution: Adding the reference changes Q to Q+1, so J=P²+(Q+1)²=I+1+2 sin φ. Therefore cos φ=(I−5)/4 and sin φ=(J−I−1)/2. For I=37/5,J=10 these are 3/5 and 4/5, locating a unique phase modulo 2π in the first quadrant (tan φ=4/3). A pair of exact readings is compatible precisely when ((I−5)/4)²+((J−I−1)/2)²=1; each point of this unit circle defines a phase and reproduces both readings. For I=5,J=6 both coordinates would be 0, violating the identity. That rejects the joint assumptions/data; it does not identify which physical assumption failed.
hints: Compare J with I before expanding the unchanged coordinate again.
Any decoded sine/cosine pair must lie on the unit circle.

extensions.gate: Integration and, for the last comparison, a specified phase probability law.
extensions.prompt: Prove the supplied period averages by integration over [0,2π]. Then suppose the relative phase is uniformly distributed on [0,2π) across long observation blocks, each with a stable phase and a full-period average. What is the mean brightness for A=2 and B=1?
extensions.solution: The identities sin² t=(1−cos 2t)/2, cos² t=(1+cos 2t)/2 and sin t cos t=sin 2t/2 integrate to averages 1/2,1/2,0 on a full period. At each fixed phase the already-derived brightness is 5+4 cos φ. Uniform phase averaging gives (1/(2π))∫₀²π(5+4 cos φ)dφ=5. This is a precisely specified block-average model for loss of coherence, not the same as assigning brightness 5 to every coherent phase.

families.title: A sales pitch that balances energy and still fails
families.core_gate: Fractions, algebraic inequalities and a clear heat/work sign convention. The second-law entropy inequality is a supplied physical law, not derived from token accounting.
families.index_gate: Heat/work algebra with a supplied entropy law; certify losses and compare cascades
families.extension_gate: Reverse-cycle bookkeeping for a refrigerator. No microscopic derivation of thermodynamics is asserted.
families.reading: Reservoir temperatures are positive kelvin values. Qh and Qc denote positive heat magnitudes in the stated directions; W is positive work output.
families.materials: Reservoir and engine diagram cards, pencil, optional twelve equal heat tokens. This is a paper model of complete cycles; no hot substances or physical machine is needed.
families.timing: 0–10 sort chosen heat/work claims; 10–25 prove the upper bound; 25–40 compare two-stage designs; later 20 minutes for entropy generation and refrigerator extension. Keep the supplied physical law beside every ledger.
families.launch: A machine returns to its original state after every cycle. Can a claim balance every unit of energy and still violate a physical constraint?
families.satisfying_stop: A sharp bound, a reversible cascade achieving the same ideal bound, and an exact formula converting entropy generation into lost work for the specified reservoirs.
families.prior_use: AP-11 also uses conservation, but here a second independent thermodynamic inequality rejects energy-balanced proposals. No prior circle thermodynamic cycle is documented.

families.mathematical_connection: Intersecting a conservation affine line with an inequality gives a sharp certificate. Reversible intermediate exchanges telescope; irreversible entropy generation has a quantified work cost in this two-reservoir comparison.

pages.title: Which claims can survive both tests?
pages.gate: Core: supplied physical laws and algebra
pages.intro: A cyclic engine takes Qh=12 heat units from a 600 K reservoir, rejects Qc≥0 to a 300 K reservoir, and outputs W≥0. It returns to its starting internal state. Supplied laws: W+Qc=12 and Sgen=Qc/300−12/600≥0. Equality in the entropy law is the reversible ideal case.

prompts.text: Invent two energy-balanced claims: one that fails the entropy test and one that passes. Label all three energy transfers and calculate Sgen. Then audit the advertised claim W=8, Qc=4.
prompts.solution: Any nonnegative split W+Qc=12 is energy-balanced. Entropy balance requires Qc≥6. Thus a choice with Qc<6 fails, such as (W,Qc)=(8,4) with Sgen=4/300−12/600=−1/150. A passing example (4,8) has Sgen=1/150; (6,6) has Sgen=0. Diagrams have heat arrows hot→engine and engine→cold, and work engine→load. Passing these necessary laws is not a physical construction.
hints: The engine’s own stored energy and entropy return to their starting values.
Which reservoir loses entropy, and which gains it?

prompts.text: Find the largest work output permitted by both laws, and prove that every larger claim fails. For general Qh>0 and Th>Tc>0, derive the corresponding bound. What happens when the reservoir temperatures are equal?
prompts.solution: The inequality gives Qc≥Qh Tc/Th, hence W=Qh−Qc≤Qh(1−Tc/Th). For the supplied values Qc≥6 and W≤6. Reversible ideal equality is compatible with both constraints. If Th=Tc>0, Qc≥Qh and W≤0; with the stipulated W≥0 the only energy-balanced passing engine has W=0,Qc=Qh. Ratios use kelvin, not Celsius. The second law is an input; this algebra does not prove it from energy conservation.
hints: Turn the entropy inequality into a lower bound on discarded heat.
Substitute that lower bound into the energy equation.

pages.title: Can a middle reservoir beat the bound?
pages.gate: Core continuation: reversible cascades
pages.intro: Use two reversible ideal engines. The first works from 600 K down to Tm; the second works from Tm down to 300 K. All heat rejected by the first is absorbed by the second, so the middle reservoir has no net heat change over the paired cycles. Initial heat remains 12.

prompts.text: Choose Tm=400 K or 450 K. Compute each engine’s work and every transferred heat. Compare with a single reversible engine from 600 K to 300 K.
prompts.solution: For reversible stages, Qm=12 Tm/600. At Tm=400, Qm=8, W1=4, Qc=8×300/400=6 and W2=2. At Tm=450, Qm=9, W1=3, Qc=9×300/450=6 and W2=3. Both total work outputs are 6. The middle reservoir receives and gives the same Qm, and its entropy changes cancel. A single reversible engine also gives W=6,Qc=6.
hints: Reversible equality fixes the heat ratio in each stage.
Use the first stage’s rejected heat as the second stage’s input.

prompts.text: Prove the total work is independent of Tm for every 300<Tm<600. Could adding more reversible middle stages improve it? Give an argument covering any finite number of stages.
prompts.solution: Qm=12 Tm/600 and Qc=Qm×300/Tm=6, so W1+W2=(12−Qm)+(Qm−6)=6. For a descending sequence T0=600>T1>…>Tn=300, reversible equality gives Qi=Qi−1 Ti/Ti−1. Multiplication telescopes to Qn=12 Tn/T0=6. Summing work differences gives 12−6=6. This covers every finite reversible cascade with no net middle-reservoir storage; adding stages cannot exceed the same external-reservoir bound.
hints: Multiply consecutive temperature ratios.
Add the work ledgers and cancel internal heat transfers.

pages.title: Locate the lost work
pages.gate: Core continuation: entropy generation as a certificate
pages.intro: Use Tm=400 K. A changed first engine takes 12 from 600 K but rejects 9 to 400 K. The second engine is reversible and accepts all 9, then rejects heat to 300 K. Both engines are cyclic; the middle reservoir has no net heat change.

prompts.text: Audit each stage and compute total work, final rejected heat and total reservoir entropy change. Compare with the reversible limit. Where did the shortfall arise?
prompts.solution: First-stage work is 3 and entropy generation is 9/400−12/600=1/400. The reversible second stage rejects Qc=9×300/400=27/4 and outputs W2=9/4, with zero entropy generation. Total work is 3+9/4=21/4; the reversible limit is 6, so the shortfall is 3/4. External reservoir entropy change is (27/4)/300−12/600=1/400, agreeing with the sum of stage values; middle terms cancel. The first stage creates the positive entropy generation.
hints: First audit the two stages separately, then cancel the middle transfers.
The second engine sees an input of 9, not 12.

prompts.text: For any cyclic device or cascade exchanging heat only with fixed Th and Tc, keep the same Qh and define Sgen=Qc/Tc−Qh/Th. Derive an exact relation between Sgen and the work shortfall from the reversible bound. Can adding a reversible stage erase already positive total entropy generation?
prompts.solution: Let Wrev=Qh(1−Tc/Th) and W=Qh−Qc. Subtracting gives Wrev−W=Qc−Qh Tc/Th=Tc Sgen. With fixed Qh,Th,Tc, positive total entropy generation forces a strictly positive shortfall, and equality of work with the reversible bound requires Sgen=0. A reversible added stage has zero entropy generation, so it cannot cancel a positive amount; all allowed stage generations are nonnegative. Changing external reservoirs or heat budget changes the comparison and must be stated. In the example 300×(1/400)=3/4.
hints: Subtract the two work expressions before replacing anything.
Keep the external reservoirs fixed when comparing designs.

extensions.gate: Algebra and a reversed heat/work convention.
extensions.prompt: A refrigerator extracts Qc>0 from a cold reservoir Tc and deposits Qh into a hot reservoir Th>Tc, using positive work input Win. Derive the least permitted input and the greatest coefficient of performance Qc/Win. Evaluate Qc=6, Tc=300 K, Th=600 K.
extensions.solution: Energy gives Qh=Qc+Win. Reservoir entropy is Qh/Th−Qc/Tc≥0, giving Win≥Qc(Th/Tc−1)=Qc(Th−Tc)/Tc. Thus Qc/Win≤Tc/(Th−Tc), with reversible equality. Here Win≥6 and the coefficient is at most 1. Directions differ from the engine: cold→refrigerator, work→refrigerator, refrigerator→hot. The positive-input premise excludes division by zero, since Th>Tc and Qc>0.

families.core_gate: Normalized two-component vectors, dot products, squared probabilities and branch trees. The Born probability and projection-update rules are supplied as actual quantum model assumptions.

pages.title: Choose the order, keep the state
pages.gate: Core: dot products and branch probabilities
pages.intro: Start with the normalized real state ψ=e0=(1,0). Define e1=(0,1). Z measures in {e0,e1}; X measures in {+,−}, where ±=(1,±1)/√2. Supplied rule: outcome b has probability (b·ψ)², then the state becomes b. Branch probabilities multiply; disjoint branches add. No evolution occurs between questions.

prompts.text: Choose X then Z or Z then X. Build its full outcome tree, labeling every branch probability and every new state. Then build the other order. In each experiment, record the Z answer wherever it occurs. How often is that answer e1?
prompts.solution: For X→Z, the first outcomes + and − each have probability 1/2. From either, Z=e0 or e1 each has probability 1/2. All four joint branches have probability 1/4, so recorded Z=e1 has probability 1/2. For Z→X, the first Z is e0 with probability 1 and e1 with probability 0; from e0, X is + or − with probability 1/2. Hence its recorded Z=e1 probability is 0. Zero-probability branches need not be continued. These are different recorded statistics; no claim is made that the final unconditional mixed states differ for these particular two bases.
hints: Square the dot product before using it as a probability.
The second question uses the branch’s new state.

prompts.text: Check that probabilities sum to 1 at every live branch. A proposed shortcut computes both questions from the original e0 and never updates it. Find a specific branch whose probability that shortcut gets wrong.
prompts.solution: Each orthonormal basis has squared projections summing to ||ψ||²=1. Explicitly 1/2+1/2=1 for the cross-basis transitions, and 1+0=1 for Z from e0. In X→Z, after the + branch the correct conditional probability of Z=e1 is 1/2; the shortcut uses e0 again and gets 0. Its joint (+,e1) probability 0 contradicts the correct 1/4. This isolates the missed update rather than a generic failure of classical probability arithmetic.
hints: Look at the state immediately after the first X outcome.
Which part of the supplied rule did the shortcut discard?

pages.title: A certain answer can become uncertain
pages.gate: Core continuation; matrices in prompt 4
pages.intro: Every run again starts in e0. Compare a repeated question with a question inserted between repeats. An outcome may be unreported, but the projection update still occurs.

prompts.text: Choose Z→Z or Z→X→Z. Predict whether the final Z can differ from the first, then compute the exact probability. If the middle X result is erased from the record, does the final Z distribution return to certainty?
prompts.solution: Z→Z always gives e0 then e0, so change probability 0. Z→X→Z starts with e0 certainly; X gives ± with probability 1/2 and each then gives e1 with probability 1/2. The final answer differs with probability 1/2. Erasing the classical X label means summing the two branches, not undoing their physical state updates, so it remains 1/2. Repeating one basis immediately is stable; inserting another basis changes the subsequent statistics.
hints: Deleting a label and deleting an interaction are different operations.
Sum the unreported branches only after updating their states.

prompts.text: Matrix gate: let P0=[[1,0],[0,0]] and P+=[[1,1],[1,1]]/2. Compute P0P+ and P+P0. Applied to e0, the squared norm of each unnormalized vector is the probability of its ordered pair of selected outcomes. Match the two results with your trees.
prompts.solution: P0P+=[[1/2,1/2],[0,0]] while P+P0=[[1/2,0],[1/2,0]], so they do not commute. Acting on e0 gives (1/2,0) and (1/2,1/2), with squared norms 1/4 and 1/2. Since the rightmost matrix acts first, these are respectively X=+ then Z=e0, and Z=e0 then X=+. They agree with the corresponding tree branches. Normalizing the intermediate state and multiplying conditional probabilities gives the same result because the intermediate norm factors cancel. A zero intermediate vector represents a zero-probability branch.
hints: Read matrix products from right to left when they act on a state.
Keep vectors unnormalized only for the stated branch-probability calculation.

pages.title: Choose the most disruptive single question
pages.gate: Continuation: trigonometry and a sharp bound
pages.intro: Start in e0, ask ONE intermediate question Y, do not retain its outcome, then ask Z. Choose Y’s orthonormal basis b0=(cos θ,sin θ), b1=(−sin θ,cos θ), with 0≤θ≤π/2. The target is final Z=e1.

prompts.text: First test the rational basis b0=(3/5,4/5), b1=(−4/5,3/5). Find the target probability using both intermediate branches. Is it larger or smaller than inserting X?
prompts.solution: The first probabilities are (b0·e0)²=9/25 and (b1·e0)²=16/25. From b0, final e1 has probability 16/25; from b1, 9/25. Total target probability is 2×9×16/625=288/625. It is less than 1/2 because 576<625. Inserting X corresponds to θ=π/4 and gives 1/2. Both basis vectors are unit and perpendicular: (3/5)(−4/5)+(4/5)(3/5)=0.
hints: Calculate the two joint target branches separately.
Compare the fraction exactly, without rounding.

prompts.text: Design the angle θ that makes final Z=e1 as likely as possible. Prove that no SINGLE unreported intermediate projective question in this real model can do better. Can the target become certain?
prompts.solution: The probability is cos² θ sin² θ+sin² θ cos² θ=2 sin² θ cos² θ. Put p=sin² θ∈[0,1]. Then 2p(1−p)=1/2−2(p−1/2)²≤1/2, with equality exactly p=1/2. On the given angle interval this is θ=π/4, the X basis up to outcome signs/labels. It cannot make the target certain. The bound is only for one unreported intermediate basis with no feedback or additional evolution; prompt 1’s order effect is not a universal 1/2 bound on all quantum procedures.
hints: A square is nonnegative.
State exactly how many intermediate questions your argument covers.

extensions.gate: Trigonometric dot products and complete probability-tree summation.
extensions.prompt: Allow TWO unreported intermediate questions, with basis angles π/6 then π/3, followed by Z. Starting at e0, can the probability of final e1 exceed the single-question bound? Derive it without selecting only favorable records.
extensions.solution: Let b(α)=(cos α,sin α) and its perpendicular partner define each basis. Transition probabilities between angles α and β are cos²(β−α) for keeping the basis label and sin²(β−α) for switching it. At α=π/6, plus-label probability is 3/4. At β=π/3 the angle difference is π/6, so plus-label probability becomes (3/4)(3/4)+(1/4)(1/4)=5/8; minus is 3/8. Final Z=e1 has probability (5/8)sin²(π/3)+(3/8)cos²(π/3)=15/32+3/32=9/16>1/2. All intermediate records were summed; no postselection or feedback was used. This does not contradict a bound explicitly limited to one intermediate question.

families.core_gate: Four binary choices, complete counting and weighted probabilities. Distinguish the weight of one configuration from total weight of a class; arithmetic reaches 82.

families.extension_gate: Exponentials connect the stipulated weights to Ising energy; binomial/parity algebra gives general finite chains and rings. No finite-system phase transition is claimed.
families.reading: An open row has exactly three interaction links. A ring adds a fourth link. Spin labels are + and −, not magnetic field directions in a laboratory setup.

families.timing: 0–12 make and compare configurations; 12–30 organize a complete catalog; 30–45 design and prove the sampler; later 25 minutes for the ring and conditional sampling. Do not require drawing sixteen near-identical pictures if a bijective encoding replaces them.
families.launch: A perfectly aligned row gets more weight than any one mixed row. Does it beat all mixed rows taken together? Can you generate exactly the right distribution without making a large weighted ticket bag?

pages.title: A favorite arrangement or a favorite class?
pages.gate: Core: four spins and weighted counts
pages.intro: Four labeled sites 1,2,3,4 form an OPEN row, with links 12,23,34 only. Each spin is + or −. If a configuration has a agreeing links, assign weight 2^a. Probability equals its weight divided by the total weight of all configurations.

prompts.text: Choose several configurations, including two with the same number of + spins but different neighbor patterns. Find their agreeing links and weights. Does counting + spins alone determine the weight?
prompts.solution: Every chosen pattern is checked along the three specified links. Examples ++−− has a=2 and weight 4, while +−+− has a=0 and weight 1; both have two + spins. Thus number of + spins alone does not determine weight. ++++ and −−−− have a=3 and weight 8; +++− has a=2 and weight 4. Global sign reversal preserves every agreement and hence the weight.
hints: Mark each link as agree or disagree.
Keep the number of + spins fixed while rearranging their positions.

prompts.text: Predict which agreement class has the greatest TOTAL weight. Organize all configurations by a=0,1,2,3, without counting any twice. Compare the probability of perfect alignment in this model with uniform choice of the sixteen configurations.
prompts.solution: Class multiplicities for a=0,1,2,3 are 2,6,6,2. Total class weights are 2,12,24,16, summing to 54. The a=2 class has greatest total weight 24, although each aligned configuration individually has the greatest weight 8. Perfect alignment has probability 16/54=8/27, compared with 2/16=1/8 under uniform sampling. The remaining mixed configurations together have weight 38>16. Any complete nonduplicated catalog or the encoding proof developed on page 2 is accepted.
hints: Pair each pattern with its global sign reversal.
A class’s total weight is its size times one member’s weight.

pages.title: Replace a large raffle by tiny choices
pages.gate: Core continuation: a bijection and an exact probability law
pages.intro: Record a configuration by its first spin and, for each link from left to right, A for agree or D for disagree. The later spins must be reconstructed from that record.

prompts.text: Prove that this record determines exactly one configuration and that every configuration has one record. Use it to certify your class counts and total weight without checking sixteen drawings individually.
prompts.solution: Given the first spin, A copies the current sign and D flips it, so the three symbols determine all later spins uniquely. Conversely, every spin row has one first sign and one link record; these constructions invert each other. For a agreements, choose their a positions among 3 links and choose the first spin in 2 ways, giving 2 times C(3,a): 2,6,6,2. The weighted total is 2(1+2)^3=54, because each independent record position contributes weight 1 for D or 2 for A. This is a complete bijection, not only a count guessed from examples.
hints: Can two rows have the same first sign and link record?
Sum weights at each record position before multiplying.

prompts.text: Design an exact random sampler: choose the first spin fairly, then choose each link independently, with the same chance p of A. What p makes each row’s probability proportional to 2^a? Give a small-ticket implementation and prove the probability of EVERY row.
prompts.solution: For p=2/3, use a fresh independent draw with replacement from three equally likely tickets A1,A2,D at each link. Choose the first spin with a separate fair coin. A row with a agreements then has probability (1/2)(2/3)^a(1/3)^(3−a)=2^a/54, exactly its weight divided by the partition sum. To derive p, compare two records differing at one bond: the desired weight ratio is 2, so p/(1−p)=2 and p=2/3. Independent fair spins instead make all 16 configurations equally likely and do not produce these weights.
hints: Compare the chance of an A with the chance of a D.
Multiply the first-spin probability and all three link probabilities.

pages.title: Close the last link
pages.gate: Continuation: parity and conditional sampling
pages.intro: Now add link 41, making a RING of four labeled sites. Weight is still 2^a, but a now counts agreements on all FOUR links. Two configurations are identical exactly when every labeled site has the same spin in both.

prompts.text: Try to prescribe the four A/D link symbols freely and reconstruct a spin ring. Which records fail to close? Use that obstruction to find all agreement-class sizes, the total ring weight and the new alignment probability.
prompts.solution: Walking around the ring flips the spin once for each D. Returning to the first site requires an even number of D symbols; this condition is also sufficient. With d=0,2,4 disagreements, counts are 2 C(4,d)=2,12,2, and a=4,2,0 respectively. Odd a classes are empty. Class weights are 32,48,2, summing to 82. Perfect alignment has probability 32/82=16/41. The a=2 class still outweighs the aligned class. The first spin supplies the factor 2; labeling the sites means rotations are not identified.
hints: What does an odd number of flips do to the first sign?
The final link is a consistency test, not a free extra spin.

prompts.text: Try this repair: choose a fair first spin and FOUR independent links with P(A)=2/3. Reject a record if it fails to close; then redraw all choices independently until one closes. Prove that the accepted ring has the desired weighted distribution. Find the acceptance probability.
prompts.solution: A particular first-spin/four-link proposal with a agreements has probability (1/2)(2/3)^a(1/3)^(4−a)=2^a/162. The accepted proposals correspond bijectively to the 16 valid labeled rings. Their weights sum to 82, so acceptance probability is 82/162=41/81. Conditioning on acceptance divides each valid proposal probability by 41/81, giving 2^a/82, the desired ring law. Repeated independent retries yield this same conditional law and terminate with probability 1 because the failure probability after n attempts is (40/81)^n→0. Forcing the last bond after only three draws would keep the open-row distribution instead, so rejection is doing real work.
hints: Add the probabilities of every valid proposal before normalizing.
The sampler must redraw rejected choices, not silently change their last bond.

extensions.gate: Exponentials for the physics connection; binomial expansion for general finite size.
extensions.prompt: Explain the Ising energy behind b^a weights. For n≥3 labeled spins derive total weights for an open row and a ring at any b>0, and state why these formulas do not prove a finite-temperature phase transition.
extensions.solution: For an open row, E=−JΣs_i s_(i+1)=−J(2a−(n−1)). The Boltzmann weight exp(−βE) has common factor exp(−βJ(n−1)) times b^a with b=exp(2βJ); for ferromagnetic J,β>0, b>1. The four-spin b=2 choice means βJ=(ln 2)/2. For any positive abstract b, the open total is 2(1+b)^(n−1). On a ring, the number d of disagreements is even, giving 2Σ_(d even) C(n,d)b^(n−d)=(b+1)^n+(b−1)^n. The finite sums are positive for b>0 and analytic there, so no singular finite-size transition is established. A thermodynamic-limit statement would require a separate limit analysis.

pages.title: Which turn points are legal?
pages.gate: Core: a supplied spacetime rule
pages.intro: Events are written (t,x). The drawing has x horizontal and t vertical. Use units with light speed 1. A massive clock’s straight segment must have Δt>0 and |Δx|<Δt. Its elapsed proper time is √(Δt²−Δx²). Add proper times over segments. An instantaneous turn is an idealization, not an inertial segment.

prompts.text: Departure is O=(0,0), reunion R=(10,0). Choose a turn point T=(t,d) with d≠0 and draw O→T→R with both legs legal. Describe the whole region of legal turn points. Test T=(5,3), (2,3) and (5,5).
prompts.solution: For T=(t,d), legality requires 0<t<10, |d|<t and |d|<10−t. Thus |d|<min(t,10−t), the open diamond between the departure’s future light rays and the reunion’s past light rays. Nonzero excursion means d≠0. T=(5,3) is legal; (2,3) has an outward speed 3/2>1 and fails; (5,5) has both legs at light speed and is excluded for a massive clock. Any chosen interior point with d≠0 works. The boundary is not included.
hints: Check each leg separately, with forward time.
A light-speed boundary is not a legal massive-clock route.

prompts.text: Clock A stays at x=0. Clock B uses T=(5,3). Compute each clock’s total reading at reunion. Then compute the reading for your own legal turn point. Why should measuring the drawn line with a ruler give a different result?
prompts.solution: A has Δt=10,Δx=0, so τA=10. Each B leg has Δt=5 and |Δx|=3, giving √(25−9)=4; hence τB=8. For a learner’s T=(t,d), τ=√(t²−d²)+√((10−t)²−d²). The Euclidean drawing length would use a plus sign and is not the supplied Lorentzian proper-time rule. Both clocks share departure and reunion events but follow different spacetime paths.
hints: The return leg has negative Δx, but it is squared.
Coordinate time 10 is shared; proper time is accumulated along the route.

pages.title: Design a clock reading, then bound every route
pages.gate: Core continuation: algebra and a global certificate
pages.intro: First restrict to symmetric excursions O→(5,d)→R with |d|<5. Then allow any finite number of forward-time straight segments, all with speed strictly less than 1, from O to R.

prompts.text: Design a symmetric route on which the traveler records exactly 6 time units. Which target readings can symmetric legal routes attain? Can the clock record exactly 0?
prompts.solution: The symmetric duration is τ=2√(25−d²). Setting τ=6 gives d²=16, so d=4 or −4; each leg has speed 4/5<1. For any τ∈(0,10], choose d=±√(25−τ²/4), with d=0 for τ=10. If a nonzero excursion is demanded, the range is (0,10). Duration 0 would require |d|=5, a lightlike boundary excluded for a massive clock. Values can approach 0 as |d| approaches 5 from below, but no legal route attains 0.
hints: Solve for the excursion distance rather than guessing turn points.
Check whether an endpoint value obeys the strict speed condition.

prompts.text: Could a route with many turns make the traveler’s clock read more than A’s 10? Give a proof for EVERY permitted finite route, including the equality case.
prompts.solution: For every leg with Δt>0, √(Δt²−Δx²)≤Δt, with equality exactly Δx=0. Summing over the finitely many legs gives τ≤ΣΔt=10. Equality requires every Δx=0, so the whole route stays at x=0 (subdivision is allowed). Any genuine movement on at least one leg makes the inequality strict. This proves a maximum in A’s rest frame for the stated finite piecewise-inertial class; it does not compare Euclidean lengths or rely on symmetric turn times.
hints: Bound each leg by its coordinate-time interval.
When can every term attain equality simultaneously?

pages.title: Change the coordinates, keep the events
pages.gate: Advanced algebra: one inertial boost
pages.intro: Return to T=(5,3). An observer moving at speed 3/5 uses t′=(5t−3x)/4 and x′=(5x−3t)/4. This single inertial coordinate system covers the WHOLE trip. Event pairs below are (t′,x′); use the same proper-time rule.

prompts.text: Transform O, T and R. Replot BOTH worldlines in the primed grid. Recalculate A’s duration and both B-leg durations from the transformed differences. Do the clock readings agree with the first calculation?
prompts.solution: O′=(0,0), T′=((25−9)/4,(15−15)/4)=(4,0), R′=(50/4,−30/4)=(25/2,−15/2). A is the straight line O′→R′, with squared interval (25/2)²−(15/2)²=100 and duration 10. B first goes O′→T′ with duration 4. Its return difference is (17/2,−15/2), giving squared interval (289−225)/4=16 and duration 4. Thus B still records 8. T′ is B’s turn event, not an event on A’s worldline. The two return segments do not share equal coordinate durations in this frame.
hints: Transform the turnaround event as well as departure and reunion.
Subtract primed endpoint coordinates for each segment.

prompts.text: Expand (Δt′)²−(Δx′)² and prove it equals (Δt)²−(Δx)² for any segment. In the primed frame, which clock changes velocity? Explain why “each sees the other moving” does not make these two complete trips interchangeable.
prompts.solution: Expansion gives [(5Δt−3Δx)²−(5Δx−3Δt)²]/16=(16Δt²−16Δx²)/16. Cross terms cancel, so the squared interval and positive proper duration are unchanged. Future timelike legs remain future because Δt′=(5Δt−3Δx)/4>(5−3)Δt/4>0. A has constant primed velocity (−15/2)/(25/2)=−3/5. B has velocity 0 on its outward leg and (−15/2)/(17/2)=−15/17 on return, so B changes velocity at T in both frames. One inertial clock versus a clock changing inertial segments is not a symmetric exchange of entire histories. The ideal turn is the acceleration limit; its duration is omitted explicitly, not mistaken for another rest frame valid for the whole trip.
hints: Expand both squares before simplifying.
A frame moving with the outward traveler does not move with its return leg.

extensions.gate: Calculus and strict concavity; square-root endpoint limits.
extensions.prompt: Keep the excursion distance d=3 but choose turnaround coordinate time t. Find the legal interval and maximize the traveler’s total proper time. Is its least value attained?
extensions.solution: Legality is 3<t<7. The duration F(t)=√(t²−9)+√((10−t)²−9) is symmetric about 5. Its derivative is t/√(t²−9)−(10−t)/√((10−t)²−9), zero at 5. Its second derivative is −9/(t²−9)^(3/2)−9/((10−t)²−9)^(3/2)<0, so the unique maximum is F(5)=8. The function rises then falls, and its endpoint limits are √40; the infimum √40 is not attained because an endpoint would make one leg lightlike. This compares two straight-leg excursions at fixed distance, not all possible accelerations.

figures.initial_worldlines: Plot O and R and the supplied standard T only where its calculation is requested; leave learner route space. Light boundaries may be constructed by the learner in prompt 1, not a filled answer diamond.
figures.warning: No Euclidean route-length scale is labeled as proper time. Never place T on the stationary clock’s original x=0 line.

families.title: What can an orbit reveal about an unseen center?
families.core_gate: Algebra, squares, positive square roots and units. Circular centripetal acceleration and inverse-square gravity are supplied physical assumptions for the main inverse problem.
families.index_gate: Circular-orbit algebra, bounded-error certificates and an identifiable measurement
families.extension_gate: Trigonometric differentiation derives centripetal acceleration. A common unknown projection factor is a separately stated simplified observation model, not an inference from a picture.
families.reading: r is true orbital radius from the center, not diameter. v is true speed on the first two pages; w is the projected measured quantity only on the last page. Distinguish a bounded-error interval from a probability distribution.
families.materials: Supplied concentric-circle diagram, exact radius/speed cards, number-line interval workspace and a later observation-model diagram. Pencil and optional calculator; all astronomical data are invented.
families.timing: 0–10 interpret radii and model assumptions; 10–25 infer and falsify a common mass; 25–45 design a discriminating bounded-error measurement; later 25 minutes for projection ambiguity and an added period measurement.
families.launch: Three tiny orbiters may reveal the same unseen mass. Choose a first observation, make a prediction and try to catch a card that cannot fit the same exact model.
families.satisfying_stop: A parameter is inferred with an exact consistency certificate; an explicit ambiguity is exhibited and a new measurement is proved sufficient to remove it.
families.prior_use: AP-04 distinguishes a population from a restricted sampler. This is a dynamical inverse problem with projection nonidentifiability. AP-19 and AP-27 later revisit designing an extra observation under different evolution laws.
families.assessment: Promising with algebra. The observation assumptions do substantial work and must stay visible. The exact/noisy/projected cases are separate pages, not silently combined into one misleading astronomy story.
families.mathematical_connection: Inverse parameter inference, interval consistency, experimental separation and a one-parameter family of observationally equivalent models.

sources.title: OpenStax, College Physics for AP Courses 2e: Satellites and Kepler’s Laws
sources.locator: §6.6, “Derivation of Kepler’s Third Law for Circular Orbits,” equations (6.60)–(6.67).
sources.adaptation: Use small test mass, dominant central mass, circular force balance and v=2πr/T. Numerical cards, error-bound design and the common-factor observation ambiguity are derived here.
sources.checked: Reopened 2026-09-25: inspected gravity=centripetal force, cancellation of the test mass, circular-speed relation and period-based parent-mass inference. No virial or elliptical-orbit approximation is imported.

pages.title: One center, several witnesses
pages.gate: Core: circular-orbit model and algebra
pages.intro: Assume tiny test particles in circular Newtonian orbits about one fixed dominant point mass M. Gravity is the only force. Radii r and speeds v are true three-dimensional values. Supplied circular balance: v²/r=GM/r². Use consistent units with G=1. All data on this page are exact.

prompts.text: Choose any two cards: (r,v)=(1,6),(4,3),(9,2). Infer the central mass from each, then test the third. Explain why the orbiting particle’s mass is absent and why a slower outer orbiter need not imply a different center.
prompts.solution: Rearranging gives M=v²r in these units. The cards yield 6²×1=36,3²×4=36,2²×9=36, so all three are compatible with M=36. In full force balance GmM/r²=mv²/r, the positive test mass m cancels. At fixed M, v=√(M/r), so outer circular orbiters move more slowly while indicating the same mass. Agreement supports consistency with this model; it does not establish that all its assumptions are true.
hints: Solve the balance equation for the common unknown.
Keep radius and speed paired on each card.

prompts.text: Predict the speed at radius 16. Invent an exact radius/speed card that cannot fit this same M, and give a numerical certificate. Also audit the card (r,v)=(4,4). What if a labeled diameter were mistaken for a radius?
prompts.solution: At r=16, v=√(36/16)=3/2. Any positive r,v with v²r≠36 is incompatible with the same exact circular point-mass model; for example (1,5) gives 25. The supplied (4,4) gives 64, so it fails. Treating a diameter 2r as radius would double the inferred mass v²r/G. An inconsistent card identifies a failure of the joint data/model claims, not specifically a faulty gravity law, a bad instrument or a noncircular orbit.
hints: A certificate should exhibit two unequal estimates of the same parameter.
The center-to-orbiter segment is a radius, not a full crossing of the circle.

pages.title: How precise must the next observation be?
pages.gate: Core continuation: guaranteed error bounds, not probabilities
pages.intro: For this page radii remain exact, but speeds may lie in stated closed intervals. No distribution or independence is assumed. A common mass is compatible if some speed in each interval satisfies the same circular model.

prompts.text: At radius 4 the speed lies in [2.9,3.1]; at radius 9 it lies in [1.9,2.1]. Find EVERY compatible mass. Prove both that masses outside your answer fail and that each mass inside it can fit both observations.
prompts.solution: Since v>0 and M=rv² increases with v, the first interval gives M∈[4(2.9)²,4(3.1)²]=[33.64,38.44]=[841/25,961/25]. The second gives [9(1.9)²,9(2.1)²]=[32.49,39.69]=[3249/100,3969/100]. Their intersection is [33.64,38.44]. Necessity follows from the two bounds. For any M in the intersection, choose v1=√(M/4),v2=√(M/9); monotonicity puts each in its allowed interval, proving sufficiency. This is a compatibility set, not a confidence interval or posterior probability.
hints: Map both interval endpoints through the increasing function rv².
Intersection proves necessity; construct the two speeds for sufficiency.

prompts.text: A new experiment must distinguish two exact hypotheses, M=36 and M=64. You can measure speed at radius 16 with guaranteed absolute error at most ε. Find the largest error threshold below which the possible readings are disjoint. What happens at the threshold itself?
prompts.solution: Predicted true speeds are 3/2 and 2. Possible measured readings are [3/2−ε,3/2+ε] and [2−ε,2+ε]. They are disjoint exactly when 3/2+ε<2−ε, or ε<1/4, for ε≥0. There is no largest permissible ε because the inequality is strict; the supremum threshold is 1/4. At ε=1/4 the intervals meet at 7/4, so that reading cannot distinguish the hypotheses with certainty. Greater precision means a smaller guaranteed bound, not a favorable random draw.
hints: Compare the upper end of the lower-speed interval with the lower end of the other.
The intervals are closed, so a touching endpoint matters.

pages.title: A hidden projection can imitate a different mass
pages.gate: Continuation: identifiability and experiment design
pages.intro: Change the observation model explicitly. Radii are still true and exact, but the instrument reports w=qv, with the SAME unknown factor 0<q≤1 for all orbiters. The exact observed (r,w) cards are (1,6),(4,3),(9,2). This common-factor model is stipulated; it is not implied by a drawing.

prompts.text: Can these three observations determine M? Construct two different pairs (M,q) that fit all three. Describe EVERY allowed pair and give a lower bound on M.
prompts.solution: The measured products are w²r=q²v²r=q²M=36. Thus every pair with M=36/q² and 0<q≤1 fits all three cards; equivalently M≥36 and q=6/√M. For example (M,q)=(36,1) and (144,1/2), or (64,3/4), are distinct compatible models. More cards obeying the same product cannot separate M from q. The lower bound is 36; no finite upper bound follows because q can approach zero.
hints: Identify the parameter combination that actually enters the observations.
Scale true speeds and compensate with the same projection factor.

prompts.text: You can also measure the TRUE orbital period T of the radius-4 orbiter, independently of the speed projection. Its circumference is 2πr. Show that one exact period determines M and q. Decode T=4π/3, using the existing observed w=3.
prompts.solution: Circular true speed is v=2πr/T, so M=v²r=4π²r³/T² and q=w/v=wT/(2πr). At r=4,T=4π/3, v=8π/(4π/3)=6, M=6²×4=144 and q=3/6=1/2. The positive period gives a unique positive v and M, then unique q; checking 0<q≤1 audits the stipulated observation model. For these observed cards, a period producing q>1 would reject the combined assumptions. The period must be independently known in the same time units, not reconstructed from the projected speed.
hints: A period measures the time for one complete circumference.
Use it first to find true speed, then compare with the reported speed.

extensions.prompt: Derive the supplied circular acceleration from x(t)=r cos(ωt), y(t)=r sin(ωt). Restore G in both mass formulas and check dimensions. Explain which parameter is identifiable if G were also unknown.
extensions.solution: Differentiating twice gives acceleration −ω²(x,y), inward with magnitude rω². Speed is r|ω|, so acceleration magnitude is v²/r. Balancing with GM/r² yields M=v²r/G=4π²r³/(GT²). Since [G]=L³/(mass·time²), both expressions have mass units. If G were unknown, circular kinematics determines only μ=GM, even with true speed or period. Separating G and M would require independent information; this is a distinct ambiguity from the projection factor.

figures.orbit_diagram: Concentric true circles with center-to-orbiter radius segments and tangential speed arrows; labels distinguish radius from diameter. Diagram may use a clearly labeled common scale or separate local scales, never unlabeled rescaling.
